reference.source: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism (ASBMR)
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive osteosclerosis caused by loss-of-function mutations in CTSK, encoding the osteoclast enzyme cathepsin K
Osteoclasts are present but cannot degrade bone matrix collagen, so bone becomes dense yet abnormally brittle and prone to fracture
Clinical features include short stature, a large head with open or delayed-closing fontanelles, frontal and occipital bossing, and a small receding chin
Acro-osteolysis of the distal phalanges produces short, stubby fingers, and the nails are often dysplastic
Dental anomalies, a high-arched palate, and obstructive sleep apnoea from midface hypoplasia are common
Distinguished from osteopetrosis by the brittle bone, acro-osteolysis, and typically preserved marrow function without the severe cytopenias of malignant osteopetrosis
Management is supportive with fracture prevention and orthopaedic care; cathepsin K biology has informed development of antiresorptive drug targets
reference.pathophysiology: Pycnodysostosis results from biallelic mutations in CTSK, the gene encoding cathepsin K, a cysteine protease secreted by osteoclasts that degrades the organic collagen matrix of bone during resorption. Because the enzyme is defective, osteoclasts can demineralise but cannot properly break down the collagenous matrix, leaving behind poorly remodelled, densely mineralised but structurally weak bone. This uncoupling of mineral removal from matrix degradation explains the paradox of a sclerotic, radiodense skeleton that fractures readily. Impaired remodelling at the acral skeleton produces the characteristic acro-osteolysis, and defective skull remodelling underlies the delayed fontanelle closure and craniofacial features.
additionalDifferentials: Osteogenesis imperfecta given the fracture tendency
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs showing generalised osteosclerosis, acro-osteolysis of distal phalanges, and open fontanelles
Skull imaging for delayed suture closure, wormian bones, and obtuse mandibular angle
Full blood count to distinguish from osteopetrosis with marrow failure
Sleep study when obstructive sleep apnoea is suspected
redFlags: Recurrent or non-healing fractures, particularly of the long bones and mandible
Severe obstructive sleep apnoea causing hypoxaemia
Basilar skull deformity or neurological compromise
Signs suggesting marrow failure that would point instead to osteopetrosis
reference.prognosis: Lifespan is usually normal, but patients face recurrent fragility fractures, orthopaedic deformity, dental complications, and potential airway problems that require long-term multidisciplinary management.
pitfalls: Assuming dense bone is strong and underestimating the high fracture risk
Confusing it with osteopetrosis and expecting marrow failure or with osteogenesis imperfecta on the basis of fractures alone
Overlooking acro-osteolysis and delayed fontanelle closure as diagnostic clues
Neglecting airway and dental complications during anaesthesia and routine care
references: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism (ASBMR)
management: There is no specific drug therapy; management centres on preventing and treating recurrent fragility fractures with careful orthopaedic fixation adapted to the dense, brittle bone
Provide regular dental and orthodontic care and monitor for mandibular osteomyelitis and complications of the high-arched palate
Investigate and treat obstructive sleep apnoea arising from midface hypoplasia with a sleep study, ENT assessment and continuous positive airway pressure where indicated
Consider a supervised trial of recombinant growth hormone for short stature under specialist guidance
Undertake periodic skeletal surveillance for deformity and progressive acro-osteolysis
Coordinate long-term care across metabolic bone, orthopaedic, dental and airway specialists
Offer genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive CTSK disorder
